prompt: Of the general tetrahedral molecules CH3X, CH2XY and CHXYZ (X, Y and Z are different groups), which is not identical to its mirror image?

choices.text: CHXYZ
CH2XY
choices.why: CH2XY has two identical hydrogens on the carbon, so a model of it can be superimposed on its mirror image with all atoms coinciding.

choices.text: CH3X
choices.why: With three identical hydrogens, CH3X is identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: All three, because a mirror image is always a different molecule
choices.why: Every molecule has a mirror image, but most are identical to it. Only the CHXYZ type can't be superimposed on its mirror image.

explanation: The CH3X and CH2XY molecules are identical to their mirror images and thus are not handed: a model of each can be superimposed on a model of its mirror image so that all atoms coincide. The CHXYZ molecule is not identical to its mirror image, just as a left hand can't be superimposed on a right hand (Figure 5.1.1).

choices.text: A stereoisomer that is not identical to its mirror image
A constitutional isomer, with its atoms connected in a different order
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same connections between atoms; they are a kind of stereoisomer, differing only in three-dimensional arrangement.

choices.text: Any molecule together with its mirror image
choices.why: Every molecule has a mirror image, but CH3X and CH2XY are identical to theirs. An enantiomer is one that isn't.

choices.text: A molecule that can be superimposed on its mirror image
choices.why: That describes a molecule that is not handed, such as CH2XY. Enantiomers can't be superimposed on their mirror images.

explanation: A molecule that is not identical to its mirror image is a kind of stereoisomer called an enantiomer (from the Greek enantio, meaning "opposite"). Enantiomers are related to each other as a right hand is related to a left hand.

prompt: According to Section 5.1, when do enantiomers result?

choices.text: Whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents
Whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to at least two different substituents
choices.why: CH2XY has two different substituents (X and Y) besides its hydrogens, yet it is identical to its mirror image. All four groups must differ.

choices.text: Whenever a carbon is bonded to an oxygen or a halogen
choices.why: CH3X can have any heteroatom as X and still be identical to its mirror image. What matters is four different groups, not which atoms.

choices.text: Only when a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to three different groups and a hydrogen
choices.why: One of the four groups need not be H; any four different substituents give enantiomers.

explanation: Enantiomers result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (one need not be H), as in the CHXYZ molecule of Figure 5.1.1.

prompt: How many different substituents must a tetrahedral carbon carry for the molecule to exist as a pair of enantiomers?
explanation: Enantiomers result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents. With any two the same, as in CH2XY or CH3X, the molecule is identical to its mirror image.

prompt: A carbon is bonded to F, Cl, Br and I (CFClBrI), with no hydrogen at all. Does this molecule exist as a pair of enantiomers?

choices.text: Yes; the carbon is tetrahedral with four different substituents, and none of them needs to be H
No; a handed molecule must have a hydrogen on the central carbon, as in CHXYZ
choices.why: CHXYZ is just one example. Enantiomers result whenever a tetrahedral carbon has four different substituents, and one need not be H.

choices.text: No; halogens are all in the same group, so they count as the same substituent
choices.why: F, Cl, Br and I are four different atoms, so they are four different substituents.

choices.text: Yes, but only because the molecule contains halogens
choices.why: Halogens aren't required; lactic acid is handed with −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CO2H. The cause is four different groups.

explanation: Enantiomers result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (one need not be H). CFClBrI meets that condition, so it is not identical to its mirror image.

prompt: Which of these molecules exists as a pair of enantiomers?

choices.text: CHBrClF
CH2BrCl
choices.why: This is a CH2XY molecule: its two hydrogens are identical, so it is identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: CH3Cl
choices.why: This is a CH3X molecule, which is identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: CHCl2Br
choices.why: Two of the four substituents are Cl, so the carbon doesn't have four different groups.

explanation: CHBrClF is a CHXYZ molecule: its tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (H, Br, Cl, F), so it can't be superimposed on its mirror image. The others each have two identical substituents.

prompt: Which analogy does Section 5.1 use for how a pair of enantiomers are related?

choices.text: A right hand and a left hand
Two right hands
choices.why: Two right hands are identical and can be superimposed. Enantiomers can't be, like a right hand and a left hand.

choices.text: A hand and a foot
choices.why: A hand and a foot are different objects altogether. Enantiomers have the same atoms and connections and are mirror images of each other.

choices.text: A hand and a photograph of the same hand
choices.why: A photograph is a flat copy, not a mirror image. Enantiomers are three-dimensional mirror images that can't be superimposed.

explanation: Enantiomers are related to each other as a right hand is related to a left hand. You can't superimpose a CHXYZ molecule on its mirror image for the same reason you can't superimpose a left hand on a right hand: they simply aren't the same.

prompt: Lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)CO2H, exists as a pair of enantiomers. Which four groups are bonded to its central carbon?

choices.text: −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CO2H
−H, −H, −OH and −CO2H
choices.why: The central carbon has only one hydrogen; the CH3 group is the fourth substituent. Two hydrogens would make the molecule identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: −OH, −CH3, −CO2H and −CH2OH
choices.why: The central carbon is CH(OH): its four groups are −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CO2H.

choices.text: −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CH3
choices.why: Lactic acid has one methyl group; the other end of the molecule is a −CO2H group. Two methyls would not give enantiomers.

explanation: Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) exists as a pair of enantiomers because there are four different groups (−H, −OH, −CH3, −CO2H) bonded to the central carbon atom.

prompt: Which statement about the two enantiomers of lactic acid is correct?

choices.text: They are called (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid; both are found in sour milk, but only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue
Both enantiomers occur in muscle tissue, but only (−)-lactic acid is found in sour milk
choices.why: It is the other way round: both are found in sour milk, and only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue.

choices.text: They are identical, since they have the same groups bonded to the same carbon
choices.why: Having the same four groups is exactly what lets them be mirror images; their three-dimensional arrangements differ and can't be superimposed.

choices.text: Only (−)-lactic acid occurs in muscle tissue
choices.why: The enantiomer found in muscle tissue is (+)-lactic acid.

explanation: The enantiomers of lactic acid are called (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid. Both are found in sour milk, but only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue.

prompt: You try to superimpose (+)-lactic acid on (−)-lactic acid and line up the −H and −CO2H groups. What happens to the other two groups?

choices.text: They don't match: the −OH of one sits where the −CH3 of the other is
They match as well, so the two molecules turn out to be identical
choices.why: If they matched, the molecules would be superimposable and not enantiomers. Matching any two groups always leaves the other two swapped.

choices.text: They match after the whole molecule is turned over
choices.why: Turning the molecule over moves the −H and −CO2H out of alignment again. Regardless of how the molecules are oriented, they aren't identical.

choices.text: Only the −CH3 groups fail to match; the −OH groups line up
choices.why: Once −H and −CO2H line up, only two positions remain, so if one group is out of place the other must be too.

explanation: You can't superimpose a molecule of (+)-lactic acid on a molecule of (−)-lactic acid. If any two groups match up, say −H and −CO2H, the remaining two groups don't match (Figure 5.1.2). Regardless of how the molecules are oriented, they aren't identical.

prompt: What does it mean to say that a CH2XY molecule is identical to its mirror image?

choices.text: A model of the molecule can be placed on a model of its mirror image so that all atoms coincide
The molecule has no mirror image
choices.why: Every molecule has a mirror image. For CH2XY the mirror image just happens to be the same molecule.

choices.text: The mirror image looks the same only when drawn flat on paper
choices.why: The test is three-dimensional: real models of CH2XY and its mirror image can be superimposed.

choices.text: The mirror image has X and Y swapped, so it is a different isomer
choices.why: Swapping positions in the mirror only gives a different molecule when all four groups differ. With two identical hydrogens, CH2XY's mirror image can be turned to match it exactly.

explanation: If you make a molecular model of CH3X or CH2XY and of its mirror image, you find that you can superimpose one on the other so that all atoms coincide. These molecules are identical to their mirror images and thus are not handed (Figure 5.1.1).

prompt: A molecule has exactly one tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups, as in lactic acid. How many enantiomers make up its mirror-image pair?
explanation: A molecule of the CHXYZ type and its non-superimposable mirror image form a pair of enantiomers, like a right hand and a left hand. Lactic acid, for example, exists as (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid.
